system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker LOSS_RPP25 (loss of RPP25 expression).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

input.mechanism: RPP25L is a paralog of RPP25, a subunit of the RNase P/MRP nuclease complex (tRNA/rRNA processing). When RPP25 expression is lost, cells rely on RPP25L to supply the catalytic-complex subunit function, so RPP25L knockout is selectively lethal in RPP25-loss lines (synthetic lethality via paralog buffering).

input.mechanism: RPP25L is a paralog of RPP25, a subunit of the RNase P/MRP nuclease complex (tRNA/rRNA processing). output: Registered H1: LOSS_RPP25 -> more dependent on RPP25L. Discovery evidence frozen: t=-23.89, n_altered=141. Replication budget left: 5. Replication passes only if one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens.

findings.claim: Cancers with LOSS_RPP25 (RPP25 expression loss, ~23% of discovery lines) depend selectively on the paralog RPP25L (RNase P/MRP subunit); RPP25L knockout is strongly lethal in altered lines (mean effect -1.09 vs -0.28 in others), holds within every lineage, replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=2.5e-59) and independent Sanger screens (p=4.6e-15).

input.summary: Top candidate: RPP25L, the paralog of RPP25, for cancers with LOSS_RPP25. In 141 discovery lines with RPP25 loss, RPP25L knockout was the most selective dependency in the dataset (lineage-adjusted t=-23.9, 134/141 altered lines strongly dependent vs 67/477 others). The effect held within each lineage tested and was not driven by one disease subtype. RPP25L is not broadly essential, so it has a plausible therapeutic window. The association replicated in 87 held-out Broad lines (p=2.5e-59) and 24 altered lines in independent Sanger screens (p=4.6e-15). The mechanism is paralog buffering: RPP25L likely substitutes for RPP25 in the RNase P/MRP complex. The novelty rating is partially known because paralog synthetic lethality is a recognised concept, but I did not check the literature. Secondary signals were weaker or broadly essential (POP7, which is also in RNase P but essential in nearly all lines, and EGLN1 with only 28% of altered lines dependent) and were not tested. Confidence is 0.8; this is a strong, replicated, selective dependency, but it is a mechanistic paralog hypothesis that has not been validated experimentally.
